Benchmark dose estimation

Source: R/bmd.R
bmd.Rd

The benchmark dose (BMD) is the dose at which the response has changed from the response at dose zero by a specified amount, the benchmark response (BMR). Its lower confidence limit, the BMDL, is the reference point of regulatory risk assessment; with the convention of EFSA and the US EPA, the lower limit of a two-sided 90% interval, confint(bmd(fit)) (confint uses the level 0.90 for BMDs). Not available for fits in the BMD parameterisation (bmdpar of drmTMB).

Usage

bmd(
  x,
  bmr = 0.1,
  def = c("excess", "additional", "relative", "sd"),
  linfct = NULL,
  newdata = NULL,
  scale = c("marginal", "conditional"),
  nodes = NULL,
  vcov. = NULL
)

Arguments

x

a drmTMB object

bmr

the benchmark response, see def; a vector gives a BMD for each value

def

the definition of the benchmark response, see Details: "excess" (extra) risk or "additional" (added) risk for quantal responses, "relative" deviation, or "sd", the change in standard deviations of the response (gaussian and lognormal families, models without random effects and variance function). The default "excess" is for quantal responses only; for continuous responses choose "relative" (the EFSA default, e.g. bmr=0.05) or "sd" (the US EPA default, bmr=1).

linfct

a matrix of linear functions to identify the parameters of the dose-response curve, or a list of such matrices, as in ed; each matrix is paired with an entry of bmr

newdata

a data frame with the covariates of the curves, as an alternative to linfct, as in ed; rows with a level of a grouping factor of the fitted data give the BMD of the curve of that group

scale

with random effects, "marginal" (default) for the BMD of the marginal (population-averaged) mean curve, the mean response over the distribution of the random effects, or "conditional" for the BMD of the typical curve, with the random effects at zero

nodes

number of Gauss-Hermite quadrature nodes per random coefficient for the marginal mean; the default decreases with the number of random coefficients, from 30 for one to 5 for five or more

vcov.

the covariance of the estimated parameters, as in ed

Value

an edTMB object, as from ed, with the BMDs and their covariance matrix, entries named "bmr:curve"; print shows the estimates and their standard errors (delta method), and confint the BMDL and BMDU (level 0.90 by default).

Details

With the response mu0 at dose zero, the BMD is the dose at which the curve reaches the response

  • excess (extra) risk: mu0 + bmr (1 - mu0) for an increasing curve, and mu0 (1 - bmr) for a decreasing curve, i.e. the change relative to the proportion that can still change;

  • additional (added) risk: mu0 + bmr, or mu0 - bmr for a decreasing curve;

  • relative deviation: mu0 (1 + bmr), or mu0 (1 - bmr) for a decreasing curve;

  • sd: mu0 + bmr sigma, or mu0 - bmr sigma for a decreasing curve, with the residual standard deviation sigma (for weights of 1); for the lognormal family, mu0 exp(bmr sigma), or mu0 exp(-bmr sigma), with the standard deviation sigma of log(y), as in BMDS.

The definitions excess and additional are for responses that are proportions (binomial, beta-binomial and beta families). For excess risk, the BMD of a curve from zero to one is the effective dose ed(x, 100*bmr). The response at dose zero, and sigma, are estimated, and their uncertainty is included in the standard errors and confidence intervals. Curves that do not reach the response give NA, with a warning. The direction of the change is that of the fitted curve. With small-sample inference (see drmTMB), sigma for def="sd" is the unbiased residual standard deviation.

The relative BMD is relative to the response at dose zero, whereas the effective dose ED p of ed is relative to the range between the asymptotes; they coincide only for a lower asymptote of 0. BMDs are not available for the hormesis models and for event data (see ed).

For the lognormal family, mu0 is the median at dose zero; as the mean is the median times a constant, the relative BMD is the same for the median and the mean.

With random effects, the BMD depends on the curve it refers to. The conditional BMD is that of the typical curve, with all random effects at zero, as the effective doses of ed with random=FALSE. The marginal BMD is that of the mean response of the population of groups, the mean curve over the distribution of the random effects, found by Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Both are the same if the random effects enter the mean linearly, i.e. on b1 and b2 with the identity link; otherwise they differ, and the marginal BMD also depends on the variances of the random effects, whose uncertainty is included in its standard errors. The standard errors are for the uncertainty of the estimates, not the variation between groups. Rows of newdata with fitted groups give the BMDs of the curves of these groups, with their predicted random effects; with scale="marginal", the terms without a fitted group are averaged over.

Confidence intervals: see confint.edTMB. Profile likelihood intervals are available for BMDs without averaging over random effects, except for the models logistic and gompertz and the smoothed threshold of nec, whose response at dose zero depends on b4; otherwise Wald intervals are returned, with a message, and bootstrap intervals are available.

References

EFSA Scientific Committee (2022). Guidance on the use of the benchmark dose approach in risk assessment. EFSA Journal 20(10), 7584.

US EPA (2012). Benchmark Dose Technical Guidance. EPA/100/R-12/001, Risk Assessment Forum, Washington, DC.

See also

confint.edTMB, bmdma, bmdbayes, bmdefsa, ed, bootstrap

Examples

# 10% extra risk of immobility of daphnids after 48 hours
d48 <- subset(daphnids, time == "48h")
dmod <- drmTMB(cbind(no, total - no) ~ dose, data = d48, model = "loglogistic",
               family = "binomial", start = c(b1 = 0, b2 = 1, b4 = 1000, b5 = 0),
               fix = c(b1 = TRUE, b2 = TRUE, b5 = TRUE))
(b <- bmd(dmod, bmr = 0.1, def = "excess"))
#> Benchmark doses, excess risk:
#> 
#>         Estimate Std.Error
#> 0.1:lf1      460       103
# the BMDL: lower limit of the two-sided 90% interval
confint(b)
#> Computing profile confidence intervals ...
#>              5 %     95 %
#> 0.1:lf1 300.1731 638.5276

# 5% decrease of the root length of ryegrass, and a decrease by one standard deviation
mod <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, model = "loglogistic",
              start = c(b1 = 0, b5 = 0), fix = c(b1 = TRUE, b5 = TRUE))
bmd(mod, bmr = 0.05, def = "relative")
#> Benchmark doses, relative deviation:
#> 
#>          Estimate Std.Error
#> 0.05:lf1    0.991     0.178
bmd(mod, bmr = 1, def = "sd")
#> Benchmark doses, standard deviations:
#> 
#>       Estimate Std.Error
#> 1:lf1     1.16     0.205
